Senses.Explanation: Literally, to pick up or select (拈) and bring out (出). In its primary Chan deployment, the compound "to pick out and bring forward" (拈出) applies to a saying, case, exchange, reply, or other item before an audience. It occurs 2,519 times in 337 allowlisted texts. A master says that the Sun-Face Buddha and Moon-Face Buddha are each "brought forward again for you" (一一為君重拈出); another speaks of "relying only on one's own solid ground to bring out one phrase" (只據自家赤骨力地拈出一句子); and a student says, "today, doubting again, I cannot avoid bringing it out from the beginning" (今日重疑，不免從頭拈出). The verb also appears as the public-interview demand "try bringing it out and let us see" (試拈出看). Chan thus uses the hand-action of picking something out as a standard verb for placing recorded words and claimed answers into the public exchange.
Senses.Note: Primary Zen-loaded word-action sense; cross-checked 'pick up' (拈), 'pick up an old case' (拈古), 'pick up and hold forth' (拈提), 'raise' (舉), and 'try bringing it out and let us see' (拈出看).

Senses.PreferredTarget: physical object: take out and present
Senses.Explanation: The same graphs also denote physically taking out and presenting an object. Incense records say that a stick or portion of incense is "brought out before the human and heavenly assembly" and burned in offering; one says, "it has long been stored in a bag; today it is brought out before the human and heavenly assembly" (囊藏久矣，今日人天眾前拈出). Elsewhere a speaker says, "I remember there is a bright pearl inside my garment; I cannot avoid taking it out at the right time" and then makes a two-handed pearl-holding gesture. These passages refer to a presented object or enacted object, not to a cited saying, so they cannot be covered by the commentarial target without vagueness.
Senses.Note: Split under item 8 because the direct object is a physically presented ritual/object item rather than a word or case.

AlternateTargets: taking up an old case (in prose)
Senses.Explanation: Literally (拈) 'to pick up / hold up (between the fingers)' + (古) 'the old [ones]', i.e. (古則) / (公案), old cases: 'picking up the old cases.' It names a commentarial genre and a standard section of a master's record — a master takes up (舉) a recorded old case and adds a prose remark (his 拈, typically marked 師拈云). The corpus enumerates it inside a family of old-case commentary forms — X67n1307: (古來有拈古)、(頌古)、(徵古)、(代古)、(別古) ('from of old there have been niangu, songgu [verse], zhenggu [interrogating], daigu [substituting], biegu [alternating]') — and it is standardly paired with, and distinct from, (頌古) ('versifying the old cases,' verse comment): a master's record files (拈古) and (頌古) as separate juan (T47n1997, 圓悟佛果禪師語錄, runs 拈古上/中/下 then 頌古; B25n0145, 中峰廣錄, 卷第三拈古頌古). Whole anthologies collect them (X66n1296 宗門拈古彙集, 'Collected Niangu of the [Chan] School'), and a further commentary layer (評唱) can be built on a master's (拈古) — Wansong Xingxiu's (評唱) on Tiantong (Hongzhi) Zhengjue's (拈古) is the (請益錄) (X67n1307). As an act it is countable (B27n0152: 呈拈古十餘則, 'presented a dozen niangu') and attached to a master's name (B27n0152: 余閱雪竇拈古, 'I read Xuedou's niangu'). The same act of taking up cases for comment is also called (拈提) (354 hits / 142 files): (拈提公案如雪竇老真可謂與古人心心相契) ('in taking up cases, old Xuedou can truly be said to be mind-to-mind with the ancients') and (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者) ('few in the monasteries have taken this case up'), both B27n0152.
Senses.Note: Genre term, corpus-wide; no master bends the meaning, so a single sense. (拈古) itself: 517 hits / 155 files; the pair (拈古頌古) in direct sequence: 65 / 57 (all counts over the 462-file allowlist, XML tags/notes/rdg stripped, whitespace collapsed, punctuation retained). Distinguish from (a) the live hall verb (拈) 'to pick up / hold up' a topic or object (拈云 4412× / 236 files, 師拈云 1170× / 92 files in the allowlist), of which picking up an OLD case is the specialised case; and (b) (頌古), its verse counterpart. Also called (拈提) (354× / 142 files; quotes in the Explanation). Sibling genres in the same enumeration are attested in the allowlist: (頌古) (1075× / 264 files), (代古) (64× / 35), (別古) (36× / 23), (徵古) (17× / 9). All curated occurrences are labels, titles, TOC/section heads, or the act of composing/reading niangu, so MasterName is null (the genre is not spoken by one master in these lines).

Senses.PreferredTarget: to pick up and bring forward
Senses.Explanation: The first graph means to pinch or pick up; the second means to lift or bring forward. In Chan records the compound names taking up a saying, encounter, case, or inherited wording and bringing it forward in speech or comment. Wumen's publication notice calls his book “forty-eight cases picking up and presenting the encounters of buddhas and ancestral teachers” (拈提佛祖機緣四十八則). A compiler's preface says descendants successively raised and sang the inherited material and picked it up and presented it (舉唱之、拈提之), then names the collected comments “statements of picking up and presenting” (拈提語). Yuanwu uses the verb for a person moving within and bringing forward the upward hinge (向箇裏出沒，向箇裏拈提). Dahui says he put two opposed statements together “without further picking up and presenting” (更無拈提), leaving students to distinguish them. Yulin says few in the communities had picked up and commented on the old woman's burning-the-hut case (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者). In a later collected comment, Dagui Xiu explicitly appraises Baofu's picking up and presenting as having considerable house style, then says that when questioned it again dragged through mud and carried water (保福拈提，頗有宗風，及乎問著，又却拖泥帶水). The term occurs 354 times in 142 allowlisted files.
Senses.Note: The same action appears grammatically as a verb, an agent noun, and a label for collected commentarial statements. Twenty-one occurrences of the agent-noun form name people who do the picking up and presenting; they are not direct definitions. The corpus relation to dragging through mud and carrying water is included because Dagui's comment draws it explicitly.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, to take up or hold up a flower. In the Chan corpus this ordinary gesture names a founding public event: the World-Honored One holds up a flower before the assembly, the gathering remains silent, Kashyapa breaks into a smile, and the World-Honored One announces that the treasury of the true eye of the teaching is entrusted to Mahakashyapa. The graph variant “holding up the flower” written with the traditional flower graph records the same event. Chan texts explicitly place it inside the lineage: one says that by the World-Honored One's holding up the flower, the wondrous mind was transmitted to Kashyapa, paired with Bodhidharma's facing the wall and entrusting the lineage purport to Shenguang. Another public address pairs locations and labels: “at the Vulture Peak assembly it was called holding up the flower; before Shaoshi Peak it was named obtaining the marrow.” Masters also question and censure the inherited event. A monk asks why Radiant Light—Kashyapa—smiled on seeing the flower held up; Daoning answers, “he could not suppress a grin.” Another record says that the flower-holding smile became a track, and yet another says that avoiding the flower-holding smile would have avoided an empty breaking of the face and the snow-standing scene becoming a rut. The deviation is therefore visible in the record: holding up a flower is not merely handling a plant but the name of a repeatedly cited, transmitted, compared, questioned, and criticized Chan case.
Senses.Note: The common flower graph and traditional flower graph are orthographic variants in this case family; they are not separate senses. The entry treats the compact event-name through the recorded assembly actions, lineage statements, naming formulas, questions, answers, and later criticism.

Senses.PreferredTarget: holding up the flower and smiling
Senses.Explanation: Literally, holding up (拈) a flower (華) and faintly smiling (微笑): "holding up the flower and smiling." The exact traditional-flower form occurs 36 times in 26 allowlisted texts; the common-flower graph variant "holding up the flower and smiling" (拈花微笑) occurs 163 times in 102. In the Chan Buddha's defining lineage scene, the World-Honored One holds up a flower before the assembly at Vulture Peak; the multitude is at a loss, while Kashyapa breaks into a smile. The recorded Buddha then entrusts Kashyapa with "the treasury of the true teaching eye, the wondrous mind of extinction, the subtle gate of the real mark without a mark, not established in written words, transmitted separately outside teachings" (正法眼藏、涅槃玅心、實相無相微玅法門，不立文字，教外別傳). Later masters repeatedly quote and challenge the scene. Yue Lin says that at precisely the moment the Buddha holds up the flower and Kashyapa smiles, both deserve thirty blows. Dongshan Shouchu says people know only the flower and smile but do not know the World-Honored One. Yulin calls it the single transmission of the treasury of the true teaching eye, then says it has made clear-eyed people laugh ever since. Zen thus defines its Buddha chiefly through this public action, Kashyapa's visible response, the assembly's failure to respond, and the announced entrustment; the later critical comments are part of the same Zen deployment, not outside hagiography.
Senses.Note: The flower graphs "flower" (華) and its common variant "flower" (花) do not create separate senses. The compact headword can name the whole recorded scene, not merely two simultaneous gestures.

Senses.Explanation: A lantern, literally a cage or basket holding a light. The word occurs 1,681 times in 293 allowlisted texts. The records use an actual lantern as a visible object: Dizang points to one, and another exchange asks which is mind after naming the lantern as form. The same object becomes a stock participant in Chan speech beside the exposed pillar: lanterns sleep, laugh, dance, listen, inspect monks, hang from pillars, or are moved into impossible arrangements. Asked what is beyond appearances, one master answers, 'a lantern'; asked the ancestral teacher's coming from the west, another points to a lantern and says, 'a very good lantern.' These are attested answers and personifications; the records continue to name the same lantern without supplying another referent.
Senses.Note: The Zen bend is the lantern's repeated use as a speaking-stage object and personified member of the monastery, especially in the fixed lantern-and-exposed-pillar pairing. The texts do not provide a mystical gloss for it. Literal object, answer, and personification remain one sense because every passage still refers to the lantern.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “lamp” and “record”: “lamp record.” The compound occurs 789 times in 91 allowlisted texts and names individual records and a family of titled compilations. Attested titles include the Jingde Transmission Lamp Record, Continued Transmission Lamp Record, Tiansheng Broad Lamp Record, and Jiatai Universal Lamp Record. Their headings and contents list masters, lineage heirs, and successive sections. A compiler’s rules says that after the Jingde collection, later compilations were named Continued Lamp, Linked Lamp, Universal Lamp, or Broad Lamp. An editorial preface says that damaged encounter wording and inaccurate comments were checked against the lamp records. These passages establish the title family, collective reference, and editorial use of the term; the entry does not assign the records a further function not stated by them.
Senses.Note: The headword-plus-transmission construction occurs 382 times in 61 texts; the headword-plus-continuation construction occurs 83 times in 13. Six apparent strings of the form “lamp record is...” are relative clauses about works or people listed in them, not self-definitions.

Occurrences.Kwic: ，烏焉成馬之失，葢所從來。統要中有機緣脫誤，拈語失真處，稽諸燈錄，裁以祖意，一皆考證的實，決無疑溷。燈譜世系既非此書所急
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An editorial preface says that damaged encounter wording and inaccurate comments were checked against the lamp records.

Occurrences.Kwic: 景德中，沙門道原所集景德傳燈錄者，其立名甚當，況有所據。後來諸師所集，或名續燈，或名聯燈、普燈、廣燈，雖各有意趣，然終欠純一
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A compiler's rules name the Jingde collection and enumerate later continued, linked, universal, and broad lamp collections.
